title: Laksa
subtitle: Malaysian coconut curry noodle soup
excerpt: Laksa is a rich, fragrant noodle soup built on a spiced coconut broth. Prawns and rice noodles make it a complete meal, and the whole dish comes together in about 25 minutes once the broth is under way.
sourceNotes: Laksa is a spiced noodle soup found across Malaysia, Singapore, and Indonesia, with dozens of regional variations. This version is a simplified coconut curry laksa, the richest and most widely known style.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The broth can be made up to 2 days ahead. Cook noodles and prawns fresh.

content.text: The broth is the heart of a laksa. Frying the curry paste in a hot pan before adding any liquid drives off the raw edge of the spices and coaxes out their oils: you should be able to smell the difference between a paste that has been properly fried and one that has just been stirred into liquid. Two to three minutes over a medium-high heat is usually enough.

Lemongrass and bean sprouts are traditional additions. If you have lemongrass, bruise 2 stalks and simmer them with the broth. Add a handful of fresh bean sprouts to each bowl just before serving. The lime juice is added right at the end: acid added earlier can cause the coconut milk to split.
Soak the rice noodles in cold water for 15 minutes, or follow the packet instructions. Drain and set aside.
Heat a large saucepan or wok over a medium-high hob with no oil. Add the red curry paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 2 to 3 minutes until the paste darkens slightly and smells fragrant.

Pour in the chicken stock and stir to combine with the paste. Bring to a simmer over a medium hob, then add the coconut milk. Stir again and return to a gentle simmer. Do not let the broth boil vigorously once the coconut milk is in.
Season the broth with the fish sauce. Taste and adjust: if it needs more depth, add a little more fish sauce; if it is very salty, a squeeze of lime will balance it.
Add the prawns to the simmering broth. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until they turn pink and opaque. Do not overcook or they will become rubbery.
Divide the drained noodles between four deep bowls. Ladle over the hot broth and prawns. Scatter the sliced spring onions over the top and serve immediately with lime wedges on the side.

items.symptom: The coconut milk has split into oily pools
items.cause: The broth boiled too hard after the coconut milk was added, breaking the emulsion.
items.fix: Keep the heat at a gentle simmer once the coconut milk goes in. If the broth has already split, whisk it briskly off the heat and it will often come back together.

items.symptom: The broth tastes flat despite following the recipe
items.cause: The curry paste was not fried for long enough, so the raw spice flavour was not developed.
items.fix: Return the broth to the heat and let it reduce for a few minutes. Add a small extra spoonful of curry paste fried briefly in a dry pan, then stir it in.
Prawns only need 2 to 3 minutes in a simmering broth. Remove them from the heat as soon as they turn uniformly pink.

items.symptom: The noodles are clumped together in the bowl
items.cause: The noodles were drained and left to sit without being separated.
items.fix: Toss the drained noodles with a tiny drizzle of oil if you are not adding them to the broth immediately. Place them in the bowls just before ladling over the hot liquid.
